conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, the book's short-side wording is the mirror. Helpers: body(i)=|close[i]-open[i]|; range(i)=high[i]-low[i]; tick = instrument minimum price move (structural constant); ema(n) = XAverage(close, n); highest(x,n,k)/lowest(x,n,k) = extreme of x over n bars ending k bars ago; avgRange(n) = average of range over n bars; overlap(i) = (min(high[i],high[i+1]) - max(low[i],low[i+1])) / range(i) (per V02's convention); barsSinceSessionOpen() = bars elapsed since today's first bar. Almost this entire chapter is one continuous 49-bar chart narrative (Figure 16.1, an ES 5-minute day) illustrating dozens of scalp interpretations using pattern vocabulary already mined in earlier chapters (double tops, ii/iii patterns, wedge bull flags, breakout pullbacks, final flags, and the always-in follow-through test from chapter 15). Only the passages stating a reusable, chart-independent test were mined here as candidates; the bar-by-bar commentary itself was not re-mined.

candidates.name: StrongTrendBarPrimitive
candidates.quote: Bar 4 ... was a strong bear trend bar and likely to form a new low of the day at a minimum.
candidates.description: Primitive: the current bar is a strong bull trend bar - bull close, body at least a fraction of its range, and small tails.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > open[0] && body(0) >= bodyFraction * range(0) && (high[0] - close[0]) <= tailFraction * range(0) && (open[0] - low[0]) <= tailFraction * range(0)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification used by other candidates in this file)
notes: Same shape as V02-01 and V15-01; redefined locally here since this file's candidates depend on it.

candidates.name: PriceLevelTouchRequirement
candidates.quote: When the market gets within a tick or so of a magnet, traders do not feel confident about the test unless the market gets that extra tick and actually touches the magnet. Until that happens, they usually will not aggressively trade it as a completed pullback.
candidates.description: Primitive: a significant price level (a magnet - moving average, prior swing extreme, round number) counts as tested only once price actually trades to or through it; a near-approach that falls short by any margin does not count.
candidates.pseudocode: touchesLevelAsSupport(level, marginTicks) = low[0] <= level + marginTicks * tick

complexity.reason: a single price-vs-level comparison with a tick margin

notes: Used via depends_on by V16-03; also generalizes the 'perfect breakout test' idea in V16-04 (a near-miss, the opposite polarity of this touch requirement).

candidates.name: MagnetTestBeforeFade
candidates.quote: with its high so close to the moving average, they would have felt more confident about their shorts if the market first touched the moving average ... Many would not have looked to short until after the moving average was touched.
candidates.description: Filter: a fade entry at the EMA (or another magnet) is allowed only once price has actually touched that level, not merely approached within a tick of it.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter gating fade entries at a moving-average magnet)

complexity.reason: adds an EMA to the trivial touch-requirement primitive

candidates.name: NearMissLevelReversalEntry
candidates.quote: The high of bar 12 was two ticks below the low of bar 3 and missed the breakeven stops on those shorts by one tick ... this would have created a perfect breakout test (perfect because it tested those stops as closely as it could without actually hitting them).
candidates.description: Price's extreme approaches within a small margin of a significant prior level (a swing extreme or an old signal bar's extreme where stops cluster) without reaching it, and the bar closes back away from that level - a 'perfect test' reversal entry.
candidates.pseudocode: priorLow = lowest(low, lookback, 1); low[0] >= priorLow - marginTicks * tick && low[0] <= priorLow + marginTicks * tick && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the market or on a small pullback once the near-miss bar closes away from the level

complexity.reason: a window lowest plus a margin-band comparison

notes: Distinct from V02-22 FailedBreakoutBelowSwingLow, which requires actually trading through the level; here the point is specifically NOT reaching it.

candidates.name: SmallBreakoutTrapReversal
candidates.quote: it reached two ticks above the triple top. If it reversed down after just a one-tick breakout, traders would have viewed that as a possible bull trap ... Bar 29 was a bull breakout of the ii pattern ... it was only a one-tick breakout and a small bear trend bar, and it could easily have set up a short.
candidates.description: Price breaks below a recent swing low or support level by no more than a small margin and then closes back above that level - a trapped-seller (bear-trap) fade entry (mirrored: a small break above resistance that closes back below is a bull-trap short).
candidates.pseudocode: priorLow = lowest(low, lookback, 1); low[0] < priorLow && low[0] >= priorLow - marginTicks * tick && close[0] > priorLow
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the close of the trap bar, or on a stop above its high

complexity.reason: a window lowest plus a capped-overshoot comparison

notes: Same shape as V02-22 FailedBreakoutBelowSwingLow but caps how far price may overshoot the level before reversing, matching the book's 'just a one-tick breakout' framing of a trap.

candidates.name: NearOutsideBarPrimitive
candidates.quote: It failed to have a high above the high of the prior bar, but with a low below the prior bar and a high at the high of that bar, it was close enough for the market to react to it as if it was an outside bar.
candidates.description: A bar whose low is below the prior bar's low and whose high reaches to within a small margin of the prior bar's high (even without exceeding it) is treated by the market as functionally equivalent to a true outside bar.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < low[1] && high[0] >= high[1] - marginTicks * tick

complexity.reason: two-bar price comparison with a tick margin

notes: Complements InsideBar in the catalog; no existing outside-bar rule to compare against.

candidates.name: CloseAbovePriorClosesRun
candidates.quote: Bar 11 closed above the closes of the past six bars (a sign of strength), and it was essentially an outside up bar at the start of a possible new bull trend.
candidates.description: The close is above the closes of each of the last N bars - a run-based sign of strength.

complexity.reason: highest over an N-bar window of closes

notes: Breakout uses '>=' against the highest close of the last N bars; this candidate is the strict '>' reading of the same test at N=6.

candidates.name: SignalBarQualityRequiredOnlyCountertrend
candidates.quote: Traders really need a good signal bar only when looking to trade countertrend in a strong trend, and signal bars often look weak most of the rest of the time.
candidates.description: Filter: require the strong signal-bar shape test only when the entry direction is countertrend to the always-in direction; with-trend entries do not need a high-quality signal bar.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (relaxes the signal-bar-quality gate for with-trend entries)

complexity.reason: 'isWithTrendEntry' depends on the always-in direction, itself a design-level context concept (see V15-02)

notes: 'isWithTrendEntry' is the always-in proxy from chapter 15 (V15-02) applied to the proposed entry's side; not redefined here.

candidates.name: BarbwireFadeAtExtreme
candidates.quote: the market was starting to form overlapping small bars with tails (which is barbwire behavior), and breakout entries would have been more likely to fail. It is usually better to buy breakouts near the bottom of barbwire and short breakouts near the top.
candidates.description: Inside a 'barbwire' region (a run of small, heavily overlapping bars with tails), fade the range: buy a breakout near the bottom of the barbwire rather than a breakout near its top.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'barbwire' classification (small overlapping bars with tails) needs a design decision
isBarbwire[0] && low[0] <= lowest(low, lookback, 0) + marginTicks * tick && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy on a stop just above the low-side breakout bar of the barbwire range

complexity.reason: 'barbwire' is a pattern-recognition judgment over variable-length overlapping small bars; no bar-level definition is given

notes: Likely overlaps the Ranges book's tight-trading-range chapter (ranges/22_tight_trading_ranges.json); recorded here since this chapter states the fade-the-extremes guideline explicitly.

candidates.name: BuyNewHighOfDayOnlyInStrongTrend
candidates.quote: Buying the high of the day is a good strategy only in strong bull trends, and that was not the current price action.
candidates.description: Filter: only allow buying a fresh high of the day when the recent bars show a genuinely strong bull trend (a run of strong bull trend bars), not merely a two-legged trading-range rally.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'strong bull trend' proxy - at least minStrongBars strong bull trend bars within the last contextLookback bars
high[0] >= highest(high, sessionBarsSoFar, 1) && countif(i in 0..contextLookback-1, StrongTrendBarPrimitive[i] (bull)) >= minStrongBars
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter on buying a new session extreme)

complexity.reason: 'strong bull trend' is a design-level judgment; the strong-trend-bar-count proxy is one workable reading, not Brooks's definition

notes: sessionBarsSoFar needs a session-open bar-count helper analogous to barsSinceSessionOpen().

candidates.name: AvoidBreakoutAboveOverlappingBars
candidates.quote: it is bad to buy above three large bars that mostly overlap. The three bars create a trading range, and it is risky to buy at the top of a trading range since most breakouts fail.
candidates.description: Filter: block a breakout-style entry above (or below) a short run of large bars whose ranges mostly overlap each other, since that run is itself a small trading range where breakouts tend to fail.
candidates.pseudocode: avgOverlap = average over i in 0..overlapBars-2 of overlap(i); isLarge = avgRange(overlapBars) >= sizeMultiple * avgRange(longerLookback); avgOverlap >= minOverlap && isLarge
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (blocks breakout entries above/below the overlapping-bar cluster)

complexity.reason: window loop computing adjacent-bar overlap plus a bar-size comparison against a longer average

notes: Same overlap() helper and shape as V02-29 PullbackOverlappingBars, applied here as an entry-blocking filter rather than a pullback-quality assessment.

candidates.name: MiddleOfDayLowMomentumFilter
candidates.quote: The market was now in the middle third of the day and was more likely to have trading ranges ... The market often lacks momentum in the middle third of the day even though the actual shape of the price action is usually reliable.
candidates.description: Filter: the middle third of the trading session tends to be lower-momentum and range-bound - disfavor breakout entries (or favor fades) during that window.
candidates.pseudocode: fractionElapsed = barsSinceSessionOpen() / sessionTotalBars; fractionElapsed >= lowFraction && fractionElapsed <= highFraction
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter on the middle third of the session)

complexity.reason: session-elapsed-fraction arithmetic against a fixed session length

notes: TimeWindow gates on wall-clock HHMM; this is a session-fraction gate, more portable across sessions of different length but needs sessionTotalBars for the traded instrument/timeframe.

candidates.name: StopClusterCascadeBreakoutContinuation
candidates.quote: They would have had buy stops above the bar 26 bear trend bar high; the bars 23, 24, 25 triple top; the bar 21 lower high; the bar 17 bull climax high; and yesterday's high. Since all of these stops were within a tick or two of each other, the stops could have been quickly hit in a cascade of stop running.
candidates.description: When a breakout bar's extreme clears several distinct prior resistance/support levels (swing highs, old signal-bar extremes, prior-day extremes) that all sit within a small tick range of each other, expect a stop-running cascade and strong continuation.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research/hard: needs a set of distinct pivot/extreme levels within the lookback
countOfClusteredLevels(levels, close[0], marginTicks) >= minLevels && close[0] > breakoutLevel
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the market once the cluster of levels is cleared

complexity.reason: requires identifying multiple distinct swing/entry-bar levels and testing whether they cluster within a small margin - swing-pivot detection over a variable set

rejected.quote: since scalping usually requires the risk to be greater than the reward, the winning percentage has to be at least 70 percent to be consistently profitable ... traders should focus on trades where the reward is at least twice the risk.
rejected.reason: trade-selection expectancy math, not a decidable bar-level test

rejected.quote: About a third of the setups are for stop entries and about two-thirds are for limit order entries ... about half of the bars have reasonable scalp setups.
rejected.reason: descriptive statistic about setup frequency, not an if-then bar-level rule

rejected.quote: Remember, a trader entering on a stop usually needs a six-tick move beyond the signal bar to be able to scalp four ticks with a profit-taking limit order.
rejected.reason: an order-fill/execution-mechanics assumption (limit-order slippage), not a distinct bar-level entry or exit condition

rejected.quote: Both the bull and the bear scalpers could therefore make a scalper's profit by entering at exactly the same time, but in opposite directions. The key is money management.
rejected.reason: illustrates two traders' differing management of the same bar rather than stating a new bar-level condition

rejected.quote: since the high or low of the day forms in the first 90 minutes or so in about 90 percent of days, traders had to look at every possible early reversal as a possible extreme of the day.
rejected.reason: a statistical fact about time-of-day, not itself an if-then bar-level test

rejected.quote: extreme scalping would be a losing strategy for most traders, and they should not attempt it, and they should never be using a risk that is greater than their reward.
rejected.reason: meta-commentary/discretionary advice about who should trade this way, no bar-level test

chapter_summary: Almost the entire chapter is a single 49-bar bar-by-bar narrative (Figure 16.1) showing how many scalp interpretations exist on an ordinary day, using pattern vocabulary already mined elsewhere (double tops, ii/iii patterns, wedge bull flags, breakout pullbacks, final flags, and the chapter-15 always-in follow-through test, reiterated at bar 26). The handful of genuinely new, chart-independent statements were mined as candidates: a magnet/level touch-completion primitive and its fade-entry filter, a 'perfect breakout test' near-miss reversal entry, a small-margin breakout-trap reversal, a near-outside-bar equivalence primitive, a close-above-N-prior-closes strength test, a rule relaxing signal-bar-quality requirements to countertrend entries only, a barbwire fade-the-extremes idea (research-grade), a strong-trend gate on buying a new high of day, an overlapping-bars breakout-avoidance filter, a middle-of-day low-momentum filter, and a hard, pivot-dependent stop-cluster cascade continuation idea. Expectancy math and execution-mechanics asides were rejected as non-bar-level.
